Airdrops Can Buy Attention. They Cannot Buy Belief.

Analysislowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 19 July 2026 · 8-minute read · Growth

Airdrops, points, ambassador programmes and referral rewards can overcome a cold start, but they also teach a community what the project values. The on-chain evidence on airdrops is consistent: Keyrock's review of 62 airdrops found most tokens fell within 15 days, and an academic study of nine major airdrops found up to 66% of claimed tokens moved to exchanges in the first transfer. Reward contribution quality and persistence, delay the largest rewards until value is observable, and count every incentive as acquisition cost.

Web3 gives companies an unusually effective growth tool: the ability to reward participation with assets, access, status or future economic value. It also creates an unusually efficient way to attract people who care only about extracting the reward.

An airdrop can overcome a cold start, distribute ownership, reward early users and create awareness. Points can make progress visible. Ambassador programmes can extend education and distribution. Referral rewards can accelerate acquisition. But incentives do not simply increase desired behaviour. They redefine what participation means. This analysis sits within our hub on building a community that lasts.

What the airdrop evidence shows

Three independent lines of on-chain analysis point the same way.

StudySampleFindingCaveat
Keyrock, September 202462 airdrops across 6 chainsMost airdrops "crash within 15 days"; 8 of 62 showed positive 90-day resultsMarket-maker research; price-based, not user-based
Messias, Yaish and Livshits, arXivNine airdrops including Arbitrum, Optimism, Uniswap, ENSUp to 66% of claimed tokens went to exchanges in the first transfer; activity rose temporarily but engagement did not lastAcademic; measures transfers, not intent
Nansen via The Block, June 2024Top 10,000 ZKsync recipients41.1% sold their full allocation within 24 hours; 28.8% held everythingAnalytics vendor; top addresses only, first day only

The academic paper adds detail that matters for design. On day one, 87% of eligible Arkham accounts, 77% of Lido accounts and 73% of Arbitrum accounts claimed, which the authors read as "strong anticipation or automation". After Arbitrum's airdrop, transactions per address fell even as total fees rose. Keyrock's work found the allocation size mattered: airdrops of under 5% of supply often held up at 15 days but dumped within three months, while larger allocations did better over longer horizons. Keyrock's winner case, Drift, combined an established user base, tiered release, a conservative valuation and seeded liquidity. Its failure case attracted reward hunters to a product with "no significant product or brand recognition".

The pattern is not that airdrops fail. It is that an airdrop amplifies whatever was already there. Where there was a product people used, some of them stay. Where there was only the reward, the reward leaves with them.

Every incentive teaches the community what matters

If a project rewards transaction count, participants will maximise transactions. If it rewards raw referrals, they will maximise signups. If it rewards posting, they will maximise content volume. The measured behaviour may grow while the underlying network becomes noisier, more expensive or easier to game.

The farming is industrial. The same paper documents a single farmer on ZKsync Era using over 20,000 accounts and deploying a fake, closed-source exchange to qualify, and notes that LayerZero offered self-reporting sybils 15% of their allocation. A design that pays per wallet is paying per account a farmer can create.

Before launching an incentive, write down the behaviour being rewarded, the durable value it creates, how it can be faked or farmed, what happens when the reward ends, which participant type it will attract, and whether it creates regulatory, disclosure or reputational risk. On the last point, the regulatory position has moved in 2026. In the US, the SEC's March 2026 interpretation said airdrops of non-security crypto assets to recipients who give no money, goods, services or other consideration are generally not securities offers. In the EU, MiCA exempts free offers from white-paper requirements, but an offer is not treated as free if recipients must provide personal data in exchange. An airdrop gated on an email address or KYC can fall outside the exemption. Get counsel on both; this is not legal advice.

If the team cannot explain the bridge between the rewarded action and durable network value, it is subsidising activity rather than growth.

Choose the mechanism for the job

MechanismUseful forRisky when
PointsMaking progress and eligibility visibleAmbiguity about future value becomes the main product
AirdropsDistributing ownership; rewarding meaningful past participationCriteria invite sybil behaviour, or retention has no independent foundation
Ambassador programmesEducation, localisation, events, member supportAmbassadors are cheap promotional labour paid for noise
ReferralsAn existing member identifying someone who will benefitThe reward overwhelms the social judgment that makes a referral credible
Access and statusRecognising expertise without financialising every actionTitles become political, opaque or detached from responsibility

Ambassadors who post about a token for rewards are also endorsers. Our piece on KOL campaign measurement covers the disclosure duties that follow.

Reward contribution quality and persistence

The strongest programmes attach rewards to outcomes a human or a well-tested system can evaluate: a bug identified and reproduced, a developer integration used by others, a high-quality educational resource, a customer introduced who becomes active, peer support that resolves real issues, research that changes a decision, governance work that improves a proposal. This is harder than counting clicks, but it aligns recognition with network value. The academic authors reach a similar conclusion, recommending rewards for value-creating users such as liquidity providers and contract creators, fee discounts for ongoing use, and multi-phase drops that refine eligibility each round.

One-time actions are easy to buy and easy to fake. Durable participation is more informative. Reward repeated useful behaviour rather than one burst, require activity across different periods, distinguish acquisition from activation and retention, create increasing responsibility rather than only increasing rewards, and delay the largest rewards until value is observable.

A person who returns after the speculative moment passes is a stronger signal than a wallet that completed fifty tasks in one afternoon.

Model the post-incentive community and the full cost

Ask what remains when the programme stops. Is the product useful? Are member relationships valuable? Has contribution created reputation? Do developers have reasons to keep building? Is there governance worth taking part in? If the answer is no, the campaign has rented behaviour. Our piece on community that survives the airdrop sets out what to build before the drop.

Crypto growth measurement should treat token incentives, quests, selective airdrops, sponsorships and programme operations as acquisition costs, not free community growth. Track cost per qualified participant, activation after receiving the reward, retention at 30, 60 and 90 days, concentration among likely farmers, contribution or revenue created, support and moderation cost, behaviour after rewards decline, and reputational effects. That is the same discipline as demand generation economics in any other market: cost per retained customer, not cost per arrival, and a CAC payback calculation that counts the tokens at what they cost the treasury.

The most important comparison is not participants before and after the campaign. It is the value created relative to the full cost, and what persists afterwards.

Illustrative example: a two-phase drop
Decision
Replace a single airdrop to all past wallets with a smaller first phase for wallets active across three separate months, and a second phase six months later weighted to liquidity provided and integrations shipped.
Reason and owner
Eligibility analysis showed a large share of candidate wallets had acted in a single week before the snapshot. Owned by the growth lead, with criteria reviewed by the engineering lead.
What changed
The first phase went to far fewer wallets, and the team could report 90-day retention by phase before committing the larger allocation.

Illustrative: a composite of a DeFi protocol, built from patterns across engagements, not a reported result.

lowob takeaways

  • Incentives define participation. Whatever you reward is what the network will produce.
  • Airdrops amplify what exists. The evidence shows quick selling where the product was not the reason to stay.
  • Pay for quality and persistence. Reward verified contribution across time and delay the largest rewards.
  • Count the full cost. Tokens, quests and operations are acquisition costs, judged against what remains at 90 days.

Common questions

Do crypto airdrops retain users?

Usually not on their own. Keyrock found most of 62 airdrops fell in price within 15 days, and academic analysis of nine airdrops found activity rose briefly while lasting engagement did not follow. Airdrops retain users where a useful product already existed.

How do you prevent sybil farming in an airdrop?

Reward behaviour that is costly to fake: activity across separate periods, liquidity that stays, integrations others use, verified contribution. Run multi-phase drops that refine eligibility, and avoid paying per wallet for one-off actions.

Are airdrops securities in the US?

Under the SEC's March 2026 interpretation, airdrops of non-security crypto assets to recipients who provide no consideration are generally not securities offers. The analysis is fact-specific and changes if the token is tied to an investment contract; get counsel.

Does MiCA apply to airdrops?

MiCA exempts crypto-assets offered for free from white-paper requirements, but an offer is not free if recipients must provide personal data or the offeror receives fees or other benefits in exchange. Gated airdrops may need legal review.

Sources and notes

  • Keyrock, Airdrops in the barren desert, 25 September 2024, updated July 2025. Research by a crypto market maker; price outcomes only; the headline 11% success rate does not exactly match its own 8 of 62 count.
  • Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: giving money away is harder than it seems, arXiv, revised 2025. Academic study of nine airdrops; some work done while two authors were at Matter Labs.
  • The Block, 41% of top ZKsync token airdrop recipients sold full allocation: Nansen, 18 June 2024. Analytics vendor data via a news report; top 10,000 addresses and first 24 hours only.
  • Sullivan & Cromwell, SEC clarifies application of securities laws to crypto assets, 19 March 2026. Law-firm reading of the SEC and CFTC interpretation of 17 March 2026; not legal advice.
  • ESMA, Interactive single rulebook: MiCA Article 4. Regulation text on free offers.
  • The mechanism table and the example are lowob's framework and illustration.

Next move

Before the next incentive goes live, write one line for each of the six questions: behaviour rewarded, durable value, how it is farmed, what happens when it ends, who it attracts and what it risks. Delay launch until the third line has an answer.
